title: Collections Framework and Data Structure Selection
learningObjectives: Explain the roles of List, Set, Queue and Map interfaces
Select a collection based on required ordering and uniqueness
Choose a queue when processing order is part of the requirement
Use maps to associate stable keys with corresponding values
Compare common collection operations before selecting an implementation

understand.concept: List preserves positional sequence, Set models uniqueness, Queue models processing order, and Map associates keys with values. Choose by required behavior and workload.
understand.whyItMatters: Collections Framework and Data Structure Selection helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a clearly labeled tool for one programming responsibility.
understand.analogyLimit: Actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## The Collections Framework as a set of contracts

The Java Collections Framework provides interfaces, implementations and algorithms for working with groups of objects. Choose an interface first: `List<E>` models an ordered sequence that permits duplicates and positional access; `Set<E>` models uniqueness; `Queue<E>` models elements waiting to be processed; and `Map<K,V>` associates unique keys with values. Map is part of the framework but is not a subtype of Collection.

## Select by required operations

Ask what the application must do most often. If it needs indexed reads and append operations, an ArrayList is a common List choice. If it needs membership checks without an order requirement, HashSet is a common Set choice. If it needs key-based lookup, HashMap is a common Map choice. If it must process the oldest waiting item first, Queue with ArrayDeque is often suitable. These are practical defaults, not universal performance guarantees.

## Ordering and uniqueness are contracts

List preserves positional order and allows repeated values. HashSet does not promise iteration order. LinkedHashSet preserves insertion encounter order. TreeSet traverses in sorted order. HashMap does not promise key iteration order; LinkedHashMap and TreeMap provide different ordering contracts. Never write a test that assumes an unspecified order.

## Consider workload and edge cases

Compare the cost of lookup, insertion, removal, traversal and indexed access for the chosen implementation. Check whether nulls are allowed, whether elements have stable equals/hashCode implementations, and whether sorted collections need a Comparator. Use generic type arguments to make the element or key/value types explicit.

## Make the choice explainable

Document the requirement that led to the choice, then test duplicates, missing keys, empty collections and ordering. Keep variables typed to interfaces when callers need only the interface contract, so the implementation can change without rewriting dependent code.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.List<Integer> list = new java.util.ArrayList<>(); list.add(3); list.add(1); System.out.println(list.get(0)); } }
examples.explanation: List preserves positional order and permits duplicates, so index zero refers to the first inserted value in this example.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Set<Integer> set = new java.util.HashSet<>(); set.add(3); set.add(3); System.out.println(set.size()); } }
examples.explanation: Set models uniqueness; adding the same Integer twice does not create a second distinct element.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Map<String,Integer> map = new java.util.HashMap<>(); map.put("apples", 4); System.out.println(map.get("apples")); } }
examples.explanation: Map associates a key with a value. get("apples") retrieves the value stored for that key.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Queue<String> queue = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>(); queue.offer("first"); queue.offer("second"); System.out.println(queue.poll()); } }
examples.explanation: Queue represents pending work. ArrayDeque's queue operations remove the head, so poll returns the first offered item.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println(java.util.List.of("List","Set","Queue","Map")); } }
examples.explanation: The four interface names summarize different contracts: sequence, uniqueness, key/value association and processing order.

practise.guidedTask: Choose a List, Set, Queue or Map for four requirements: ordered tasks, unique tags, first-in-first-out jobs and product-code lookup. Implement one example of each.
practise.independentTask: Build a small contact directory that uses a Map for lookup and a List for ordered display. Explain why a Set or Queue would not replace either structure.
hints: Write down the required behavior first: positional sequence, uniqueness, key lookup or processing order.
Choose an implementation only after checking its ordering, null and equality contracts; do not assume HashMap or HashSet iteration order.
Compare the operations your workload performs most often, then test empty, duplicate and missing-value cases.
practise.challenge: Compare the selected structures for duplicate handling, ordering, lookup and insertion requirements; justify one alternative implementation.

questions.prompt: Which interface models a sequence with positional access?
questions.explanation: List provides positional access through indexes and allows duplicate elements.
Set models uniqueness, so adding an equal element does not increase the number of distinct members.

questions.prompt: Which interface associates keys with values?
questions.explanation: Map stores associations from keys to values; it is not a positional sequence.

questions.prompt: Which type is designed for processing elements in a queue order?
questions.explanation: Queue exposes operations such as offer and poll for elements waiting to be processed.

options: Required behavior, ordering and operation costs
questions.answer: Required behavior, ordering and operation costs
questions.explanation: Data-structure selection should follow required behavior and workload, including ordering and operation costs.
